chunks: What is a stepper motor. The question: What is a stepper motor?
A stepper motor moves in small, fixed steps. Each pulse sent to its driver (the electronics that power its coils) turns the shaft by one step.
By counting pulses, you know how far it has turned, usually without any position sensor. It can also hold its position firmly when stopped.
Think of the second hand on a ticking clock. It does not sweep smoothly. It jumps a fixed amount on each tick, and counting ticks tells you the time passed.
A stepper works the same way, with each pulse as a tick.
The analogy breaks down at one point: a clock cannot be overloaded, but a stepper pushed too hard silently skips a step and loses count.
Where steppers sit in the motor family, and the subdivision inside steppers. The hybrid, bipolar stepper (NEMA 17 and similar) is the one you will meet in practice.
Step: one fixed angular move of the shaft, caused by one pulse. Phase: one of the motor's coil groups. Most steppers have two.
Holding torque: the turning force that keeps the shaft in place when the coils are powered but the motor is still.
Open loop: control by counting pulses, with no sensor to check the result. Missed step: a step the motor fails to make, so the position count is wrong.
A common stepper turns 1. 8° per step. A full turn is 360° / 1. 8° = 200 steps . To rotate a quarter turn, send 200 / 4 = 50 pulses . To rotate half a turn, send 100.
If you then stop sending pulses but leave the coils powered, the shaft stays put against a push, up to the holding torque.
That is the whole idea: one pulse, one step, and the count tells the position.
"A stepper is a brushless motor that moves in fixed angular steps, one per pulse to the driver, so you can position it by counting pulses, usually open loop.
The common hybrid type has two phases and 50 rotor teeth, giving 1. 8 degrees per step, 200 per revolution.
It has high holding torque at standstill, but torque falls with speed and it can lose steps if overloaded. Windings are bipolar or unipolar."
